body: Text-linguistics is a human-made discipline of linguistics — the study of the structure, coherence, and function of extended texts (discourses) as structured wholes that extend beyond the sentence level. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the unit of analysis is the text or discourse as an integrated semantic-pragmatic entity, governed by relations of cohesion (grammatical and lexical ties across clauses), coherence (understandable logical and semantic connections), and communicative purpose (the function the text serves in interaction); (2) the analytical tools include discourse structure analysis (narrative, argumentative, expository patterns), information structure (theme-rheme, given-new), referential continuity (pronoun chains, anaphora resolution), and textual genre conventions that organize texts for specific communicative situations. Text-linguistics persists as a discipline that produces descriptions of textual organization across languages, models of discourse interpretation, and applications in text technology, rhetoric, discourse analysis, and language pedagogy. Paradigmatic cases: Halliday and Hasan's cohesion analysis, van Dijk's discourse semantics, rhetorical structure theory. [formal: textus-linguistica | substrate: mind | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The vocal-tract model is a human-made model of the vocal tract as an acoustic filter cavity in speech production, describing how the shape of the vocal tract resonates to shape the glottal source into speech sounds. Parameters: area function along tract length, formant frequencies and bandwidths, articulatory positions. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized as acoustic tube theory, implemented in speech synthesis and analysis software, and taught in phonetics; it persists as a reusable filter component of the source-filter framework. [formal: vocal-tract | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

Psycholinguistics is a disciplinary framework for mapping the mental representations and processes underlying language production, comprehension, and acquisition. Parameters: processing models, lexical access, syntactic parsing, memory constraints, experimental paradigms, developmental stages. It persists via peer-reviewed experiments, cognitive models, laboratory protocols, and university curricula that replicate findings across populations.

Corpus-linguistics is a human-made empirical approach to linguistics — the study of language patterns, structures, and usage through systematic analysis of large, representative collections of real-language data (corpora). Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the primary data source is authentic, naturally occurring language recorded in written or spoken form (not introspective or constructed examples), organized into annotated or searchable text collections that sample from defined populations, registers, genres, or time periods; (2) the analytical methods are data-driven and statistical, including frequency analysis, collocation measurement, concordance line examination, n-gram modeling, and distributional semantics, used to discover patterns that may not be predictable from theory alone. Corpus-linguistics persists as a methodological framework that generates empirical descriptions of language (dictionaries, grammars), tests theoretical hypotheses against real usage data, and produces applications in language technology (spell checkers, machine translation, language models), lexicography, and language education. Paradigmatic cases: Brown Corpus frequency analysis, COCA/COHA diachronic corpora, Sketch Engine collocation tools. [formal: corpus-linguistica | substrate: data | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The glottal-source model is a human-made model of the glottal airflow source in speech production, describing the periodic excitation generated by vocal fold vibration. Parameters: fundamental frequency, open quotient, asymmetry coefficient, return phase. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized as mathematical equations, implemented in speech synthesis software, and taught in speech science; it persists as a reusable component of the source-filter framework. [formal: glottal-source | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

Sociolinguistics is a disciplinary framework for mapping systematic correlations between linguistic variation and social structure. Parameters: speech community, social variables (class, gender, age, ethnicity, region), linguistic variables (phonetic, lexical, syntactic, pragmatic), interactional context and language ideology. It persists via peer-reviewed publications, university curricula, research corpora, and methodological protocols that replicate observations across speech communities.

A cepstrum is the power spectrum of the log-power spectrum of a signal. Computed by: taking the Fourier transform of the signal, computing the log of the magnitude spectrum, then computing the inverse Fourier transform of the log-magnitude spectrum. Parameters: window size for the initial transform, overlap for overlap-add reconstruction. The cepstrum separates periodic structures in the spectrum (such as formant echoes in speech or pitch harmonics) into distinct peaks at quefrency positions corresponding to the delay between reflections. Persistence mechanism: the cepstrum is computed as a deterministic mathematical transform, implemented in speech analysis and audio processing software, and used as an intermediate representation in cepstral feature extraction pipelines. [formal: cepstrum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Lexeme is a human-made conceptual category — the minimal meaningful unit of a language that functions as the basic item in the mental lexicon of speakers. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) minimal meaningfulness: the lexeme carries semantic content that cannot be decomposed into smaller meaningful parts within that language's grammar, distinguishing it from phrases or complex words whose meaning is compositional; (2) identity-independence: the lexeme has a single abstract identity across all its surface forms — inflectional variants (walk/walks/walked/walking) and allomorphic variants (happy/happiness) express the same lexeme, while a shift in core meaning or derivational structure marks a different lexeme; (3) mental reality: lexemes are stored and retrieved by speakers as discrete units in the mental lexicon, not as lists of word forms. Lexemes persist as the atomic referent of grammatical description, lexical semantics, and word-formation rules. [formal: lexema | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Computational linguistics is a disciplinary framework for formalizing linguistic knowledge in algorithms and computational models. Parameters: corpus design, statistical models, symbolic grammars, evaluation metrics, processing pipelines. It persists via open-source software, benchmark datasets, peer-reviewed publications, and university curricula that replicate model performance across tasks.

Linguistic register is the map of the system of situationally differentiated language varieties a speech community develops and maintains — the varieties a community deploys for different communicative situations (colloquial, formal, technical, ceremonial, professional) — carved along three parameters. (1) The situational axis: the dimensions along which the varieties are organized are field (the subject matter and activity in which the language is deployed), tenor (the social relations and roles between participants), and mode (the channel and the participatory structure of the discourse); a variety is a conventionalized set of lexical, grammatical, and prosodic choices indexed to the situation, so that the same speaker deploys different varieties in different situations. (2) The boundary lines that separate the map from its neighbours: register is indexed to situation, which distinguishes it from dialect (indexed to region and social group) and from genre (a type of discourse text rather than a variety of the language itself); and it is distinct from the institutional register — an official list maintained by an authority with legal or institutional force — in that a linguistic register is updated by the speech community's convention, not by institutional mandate, and no authority stands behind its entries. (3) The map, not the territory: the entry names the systematic description the community and the discipline build over the natural variation of speech — the inventory of varieties and the dimensions that organize it — not the natural variation itself. Persistence: the varieties persist as social convention — acquired in socialization, maintained through institutional reinforcement (courts, academies, professions, liturgy), and relearned by each generation; the map persists as the stable sub-field of linguistics called register analysis, its dimensions codified in textbooks and corpora. [formal: regiter linguae | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

Neurolinguistics is a human-made interdisciplinary field — the study of the neural and biological mechanisms that underlie language acquisition, processing, representation, and comprehension. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory level is biological/neural (brain anatomy, neural circuits, electrophysiological responses, neuroimaging data, lesion studies, and molecular markers), not purely behavioral or computational; (2) the phenomenon explained is language in its full range — phonology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, lexicon, acquisition, and breakdown — treated as operations implemented by neural systems. Neurolinguistics persists as an active research enterprise that generates testable hypotheses about how the brain implements language, uses these hypotheses to interpret clinical conditions (aphasia, dyslexia, speech disorders), and informs brain-computer interfaces for language restoration. Paradigmatic methods: fMRI and EEG mapping of language tasks, lesion-symptom mapping in aphasia patients, intracranial electrophysiology, and computational modeling of neural language processing. [formal: neurolinguistica | substrate: brain | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Historical linguistics is a disciplinary framework for reconstructing diachronic change in language systems from attested corpora. Parameters: comparative method, sound change laws, attestation dates, textual corpora, reconstruction techniques. It persists via published reconstructions, philological editions, comparative datasets, and university curricula that transmit methodological standards across generations.

The source-filter model is a human-made mathematical model of speech production that decomposes the speech signal generation into a source component, typically the glottal airflow with fundamental frequency, and a filter component, the vocal tract transfer function shaping formants. Parameters: source excitation model, filter order, formant frequencies and bandwidths, glottal pulse shape. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized in equations, implemented in speech synthesis and analysis software, and taught in speech science curricula; it persists as a reusable theoretical framework. [formal: source-filter-model | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

Cognitive-linguistics is a human-made approach to linguistics — the study of language as a manifestation of general cognitive abilities, including categorization, conceptualization, metaphorical reasoning, and embodied experience. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory framework denies that language operates as an autonomous module separate from general cognition; language structure reflects domain-general cognitive mechanisms like attention, memory, pattern recognition, and conceptual blending; (2) the empirical evidence comes from cross-linguistic analysis of how semantic structure, syntactic patterns, and figurative language systematically reflect cognitive universals (spatial reasoning, embodiment, force-dynamics) rather than language-internal formal rules. Cognitive-linguistics persists as a theoretical framework that produces models of construction grammar, conceptual metaphor theory, and cognitive semantics, generating testable predictions about language use, acquisition, and processing that compete with modularist accounts. Paradigmatic cases: conceptual metaphor analysis (e.g., ARGUMENT IS WAR), construction grammar descriptions, image-schema theory. [formal: cognitio-linguistica | substrate: mind | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Derivation is a human-made morphological operation — the process by which a language creates a new lexeme from an existing one by adding derivational material. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) lexeme change: the output is a new lexeme with a distinct dictionary identity from the input (happy → happiness is one lexeme becoming another; walk → walked is NOT derivation, because walked is an inflected form of the same lexeme as walk). This lexeme-change criterion is the decisive boundary from inflection. (2) derivational material: the operation is carried by a bound morpheme (affix) or, in some languages, by a change of stress, vowel, or other internal modification that contributes derivational meaning (English sing → song: an ablaut-derived noun; by contrast the tense forms sang and sung remain inflected forms of the same lexeme as sing). (3) conventionalized meaning: the derivational material contributes a systematic, predictable meaning (-ness 'state of being', un- 'negation', -er 'agent') that transforms the input lexeme's meaning in a rule-governed way. Paradigmatic cases: happy + -ness → happiness (new lexeme); write → writer (new lexeme, agentive). Derivation persists as a productive rule — speakers coin new derived lexemes on the fly — and as a stable category of grammatical description: derivational affixes are catalogued in the morphological inventory of each language. [formal: derivatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
